newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian gold lustre dimmed by Bre-X row.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian gold lustre dimmed by Bre-X row.

text.p: A row between a small Canadian mining company and its Indonesian partner has tarnished some of the glitter of one of the world's biggest gold finds.

Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd jumped from obscurity to wealth on the back of the huge discovery in Indonesia's East Kalimantan province which, according to company estimates, contains more than 47 million ounces of gold.
But the government is holding up contracts of work (COWs) which Bre-X needs to continue exploration and development of its Busang property until an ownership dispute is settled.
Official sources say the COWs are unlikely to be granted soon due to the complexity of the problem, which major mining companies are watching with growing concern.

Further confusing the issue was an announcement by Bre-X in Canada that it had forged an alliance with a company controlled by Sigit Harjojudanto, the eldest son of Indonesia's President Suharto, in a deal potentially worth many millions of dollars.
Well-informed mining industry sources said Canadian gold giant Barrick Gold Corp, in association with Suharto's eldest daughter Siti Hardyanti Rukmana, had also shown an interest in Busang.
The confusion and ownership dispute has sent Bre-X's share price gyrating on the Toronto market. The stock closed at C$21.15 on Friday.

The curtain rose on the drama when Alberta-based Bre-X in 1993 took over an 80 percent share of the Busang I property -- containing over three million ounces of gold -- in partnership with Indonesian businessman Jusuf Merukh, who holds an undisputed 10 percent. Merukh claims he has a 20-percent stake through two companies he controls.

Bre-X, with another partner, proceeded to explore the adjacent Busang II and III areas, which contain the bulk of the gold-bearing ore, and last year applied for contracts of work covering these two areas -- leaving Merukh out of the deal.
Merukh argues that he also has a right to a 20 percent interest in Busang II and III with an option to buy another 20 percent, a claim Bre-X disputes as unfounded.

The original Busang I contract of work was held by Australian company Westralian Resource Project. Merukh says Westralian sold its rights to Waverley Finance Management of Scotland, which sold them to Bre-X.

Merukh bases his claim on what he says was his original agreement with Westralian. He says he has entered into a agreement with Australia's Golden Valley Mines NL to provide him with technical assistance in return for a royalty.
Indonesia's director-general of mining, Kuntoro Mangkusubroto, has said Bre-X will not get its contracts of work until the onwership dispute is settled.
Market analysts say the row is likely to affect Bre-X's search for a partner to help finance the estimated $2.0 billion needed to develop Busang.
Mining industry sources, meanwhile, have expressed growing concern over the dispute, and the involvement of President Suharto's oldest son through his company PT Panutan Duta.

Bre-X said Sigit's company would get a consultancy fee of $1.0 million a month for 40 months and a 10-percent stake in two of the richest Busang fields, dependent on the company getting its contracts of work.
Part of the deal includes a support services firm to be owned 60 percent by Bre-X and 40 percent by Panutan.
Indonesia has already caused an international furor this year by granting tax and tariff breaks to another Suharto son to produce a "national car" in conjunction with a South Korean car maker.
Japan, the United States and the European Union have complained to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) over the car deal.
Mining industry sources say their concern over Bre-X lies in the way the contract of work might be dealt with and possible political influence.
"There is a great deal of concern," one senior source said. "The contract of work mechanism has worked very well and for a long time because it has been transparent up to now."
Another source said there was a danger international companies might look elsewhere if there were doubts about working conditions in Indonesia.
A senior official source told Reuters the Bre-X situation was a unique affair, and sought to allay concern over work contracts.
Merukh, meanwhile, says he plans to fight for his pot of gold.
"By law, I have a right to Busang II and III. I want the gold, not the right. I am confident of getting my stake," he told Reuters.
